questions.q: How is RCSI different from every isolation level covered earlier in this cluster?
options: It's a database-level setting an administrator turns on once, not a session-level choice made with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL
It can only be used by the database owner, never by application code
It is actually a stricter level than SERIALIZABLE
It requires every query to be rewritten to say SNAPSHOT explicitly
questions.explain: RCSI is turned on with ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON -- a one-time database setting, unlike every session-level isolation level before it.

questions.q: What happens to ordinary application code after RCSI is enabled on a database?
options: It keeps running under READ COMMITTED with no code changes, but the engine now serves those reads via row versioning instead of locks
Every query must be rewritten to add SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT
All existing queries fail until updated
READ COMMITTED stops being the default isolation level
questions.explain: RCSI changes what READ COMMITTED means under the hood for every session, with zero application code changes required.

questions.q: What is the key difference between RCSI and full SNAPSHOT isolation?
options: RCSI gives a fresh, newly-versioned read on every statement; SNAPSHOT fixes one consistent version for the whole transaction
RCSI is session-level and SNAPSHOT is database-level
RCSI prevents phantom reads while SNAPSHOT does not
There is no difference -- they behave identically
questions.explain: RCSI's reads can see a more recent committed state on each new statement, same as ordinary READ COMMITTED always could -- SNAPSHOT instead locks in one point-in-time view for the entire transaction.

questions.q: Does RCSI prevent nonrepeatable reads and phantom reads?
options: No -- it still allows both, for the same underlying reason ordinary READ COMMITTED does; it just avoids blocking while reading
Yes, it prevents both, same as SERIALIZABLE
It prevents nonrepeatable reads but still allows phantom reads
It prevents phantom reads but still allows nonrepeatable reads
questions.explain: RCSI changes HOW READ COMMITTED reads are served (versioning instead of locking) but not WHAT READ COMMITTED guarantees -- nonrepeatable and phantom reads remain possible.

questions.q: Why do many production systems enable RCSI?
options: It reduces reader/writer blocking dramatically without requiring any application code changes
It is required before SERIALIZABLE can be used
It is the only way to run SELECT statements at all
It eliminates the need for transactions entirely
questions.explain: RCSI is a high-leverage, low-risk tuning change: flip one database setting, and ordinary READ COMMITTED queries stop blocking on writers, with no query rewrites needed.
